this amazake or amasake shop is located behind a small shrine, it is a 9 minute walk from Fushimi Inari Tiasha, aka the Senbon Torii (thousand torii gates). 

don’t ask me how I found it, it was very randomly on google 360 but the point being, this place is run by the lovely lady, Suzuki Kazuyote. her warmth and hospitality is unparalleled as you can already see in the video. 

both hot and cold amazake are available here and it is just for ¥500 which is absolutely insane. 

for those wondering, what is amazake? amazake is a traditional sweet low or non-alcoholic japanese drink made with fermented rice. essentially the alcohol percentage separates it from sake. 

if you are visiting senbon torii then you need to cool off here after the long hike (this too is about a 500 meter hike) but everything is worth the break from the tourists and having a traditional experience. it truly surprises me how lowkey this place is and it is barely on anyone’s radar.

as much as i wanted to gatekeep it, I just couldn’t resist.

Are you ready to ride Japan's iconic bullet train? Buying Shinkansen tickets can seem intimidating, but don't worry, we've got you covered!

Here's a step-by-step guide on how to buy your Shinkansen ticket and access the platform:

*Step 1: Buying Your Ticket*
Find the ticket vending machines or the ticket counter at the train station. You can choose from various types of tickets, including reserved and unreserved seats.

*Step 2: Choosing Your Train*
Select your desired train route, departure time, and seat type (if applicable). Don't forget to check the train schedule and plan your trip accordingly!

*Step 3: Getting to the Platform*
Once you have your ticket, head to the ticket gates. You'll need to go through not one, but TWO sets of gates to access the Shinkansen platform!

The first gate is for regular train passengers, while the second gate is specifically for Shinkansen passengers. Make sure to insert your ticket correctly and follow the signs to the correct platform!

*Step 4: Boarding the Shinkansen*
Find your designated car and seat, and get ready to experience the thrill of riding Japan's iconic bullet train!

Tips:

- Make sure to arrive at the station with plenty of time to spare, as the ticket-buying process can take a few minutes.
- Don't forget to validate your ticket before boarding the train.
- If you're traveling with a Japan Rail Pass, you'll need to exchange it for a ticket at the ticket counter.

With these simple steps, you'll be zooming across Japan in no time! Have you ridden the Shinkansen before? Share your experiences in the comments below!

Tokyo is a city that feels like it has everything—but when it comes to fashion, where do you even start? After exploring for a few days, I came across these 5 shops that stood out for all the right reasons:

1️⃣ Kindal (Ginza & Nakameguro) – Tokyo’s upscale thrift heaven. The Ginza location has two floors: luxury brands on the first floor, premium finds upstairs. I found this stunning @lardiniofficial coat for around $300—still obsessed.

2️⃣ QOO (Omotesando/Shibuya) – Vintage with drama. This shop is so extra, and I love it. Bold prints, rare designer gems, and bags galore—it’s a paradise for vintage lovers!

3️⃣ Amore (Omotesando/Shibuya) – ADORABLE. They’ve got so many cute vintage Chanel tweed sets, and if you’re on the hunt for one, this is where you’ll find it. Bonus: They have two locations just steps apart.

4️⃣ Casanova Vintage (Omotesando/Shibuya) – A curated selection of vintage bags, particularly Chanel and Louis Vuitton. I almost bought a classic flap here but decided rent was more important…🤠

5️⃣ The Real McCoy’s – A must-visit for Americana-inspired fashion. Think high-quality denim, leather jackets, military-style coats, and vintage-inspired tees. Ladies, bring your man here. Trust me.

Save this list for your next Tokyo trip or share it with someone who’d love these spots!

This Fukuoka udon shop serves a unique carbonara udon topped with freshly boiled noodles, eggs, and cheese.

Two rich, orange egg yolks sat beautifully on the noodles, and because the noodles are served hot, mixing them creates a creamy sauce that clings naturally to every strand✨

However, it lacked the punch of cheese and black pepper you’d expect from a traditional carbonara. Adding mentaiko (spicy cod roe) really helped enhance the flavor with its umami and mild spiciness.

You can skip the line by purchasing a Fast Pass (¥390), and reservations are also available—definitely worth keeping in mind for your visit!

추천받은 특상 쇼유 라멘을 주문했는데요, 국물은 토종닭과 4종류의 말린 생선으로 감칠맛을 더한 진한 간장 스프가 특징이에요. 스트레이트 면이 국물을 잘 머금고, 저온 조리된 돼지 차슈, 튀긴 우엉, 교토산 파, 완벽한 반숙 계란이 토핑으로 올라가 있답니다.

특히 차슈는 간장과 소금으로 각각 양념되어 부드럽고 깊은 맛을 자랑했어요. 김을 국물에 풀면 해산물 풍미가 한층 더해지며, 재료 하나하나에서 정성을 느낄 수 있는 한 그릇이었답니다.

- 영업: 월.화 휴무, 11:30 - 14:30, 17:30 - 22:00
- 가격: 특상 쇼유 라멘 (1,780엔)

Let me introduce Ramen Jazzy Beats, a must-visit ramen spot in Tokyo for true ramen enthusiasts.

I tried their signature Special Shoyu Ramen, and it was truly impressive. The broth, made with premium free-range chicken and four types of dried fish, had a rich soy sauce flavor. The straight noodles perfectly absorbed the broth, and the toppings included sous vide pork chashu, crispy burdock root, Kyoto-grown green onions, and a perfectly soft-boiled egg.

There has never been a better time to buy a watch in Japan. 

1. Low Prices
Thanks to a number of macroeconomic factors that started in the ‘90s, the Japanese Yen is really low. The watch market has not fully adjusted yet so you are able to find amazing steals. On top of this, in Japan 10% VAT is deducted straight from the price at the shop.

2. Large Vintage Market
Due to its economic prosperity in the ‘80s, Tokyo is the best vintage city in the world. Particularly if you take into consideration Japan’s attitude towards good maintenance. You will be able to find rare and unique pieces in amazing condition.

3. Watch Trends
Japan doesn’t always follow the same trends as the rest of the world as it can be quite trend insular. Popular watches abroad are still unwanted here and priced accordingly.

Most importantly just enjoy your trip and lose yourself in the experience.

Tucked away near Meidaimae Station in Setagaya, Miles is one of Tokyo’s oldest and most beloved jazz kissaten, quietly echoing the Showa era since it first opened in 1960.

With just around 10 seats, Miles offers an intimate setting where regulars and newcomers sit shoulder to shoulder, immersing themselves in classic jazz grooves. It is said that John Coltrane stopped by during his visit to Japan in 1966.

If you’re longing for a time‑slowed moment in Tokyo— Miles is your sanctuary. Be sure to stop by, quietly request a favorite record, and experience the timeless magic of Tokyo’s kissaten culture. Save this one for your next visit!

Bar Taki is a tiny jazz bar tucked away in the crowded alleys of Shinjuku’s Golden Gai. Like many of the bars here, the space is small—fitting fewer than 10 people—so everyone sits shoulder to shoulder, sipping drinks and chatting.

Loud jazz music fills the room, and visitors from all over the world gather to drink, listen, and talk, creating a close and cozy vibe. If you’re lucky enough to get a seat by the window, you can even open it and chat with guests at the bar across the way—it’s such a unique and fun experience!

It’s easy to understand why Golden Gai is so loved. Coming here to experience this side of Tokyo’s nightlife culture, right in the heart of the city, is something truly special. Save this video for your next Tokyo trip!
